title: Errors and exceptions: try, except, else and finally

videos.script:
A program that has never failed has never met a real file, a real network or a real person typing. {{normal}} Failure is not the unusual case — it is half of what a program does, and the half most beginners leave to chance.

{{value}} Python's answer is the exception. Something goes wrong, the language stops what it was doing and hands the failure up the stack as an OBJECT: a type that says what kind of wrong, a message that says which one, and a traceback that says where. It is information, delivered.

{{default}} And the default behaviour is right more often than people expect. An uncaught exception stops the program and prints the traceback — the file, the line, the call that led there. **That is a better outcome than most of the code written to avoid it**, because a program that stops has not written half a file or charged somebody twice.

{{catch}} So the question is never "how do I stop this failing". It is: **is there something I can DO about this here?** If there is — try another server, use a default, tell the person which row of their file is wrong — catch it. If there is not, let it go up. Somebody above you may know, and if nobody does, the traceback is the right answer.

{{bare}} There is one thing this lesson will ask you never to write, and it is `except:` with nothing after it. It catches everything, including the interrupt you press Ctrl-C for, and it turns a message that named the file and the line into silence. A program that fails loudly is being kind to you; one that fails quietly is not.

{{four}} Four clauses — `try`, `except`, `else`, `finally` — and each has one job. Then raising your own, which is how a library says something useful rather than letting a `KeyError` escape from three layers down with no idea what it meant.

{{eafp}} And a habit that will look strange and is deeply Pythonic: try it and catch the failure, rather than checking first. There is a section on why, and the reason is not style.

The same bug, three ways. A configuration file with a typo in it — a port written as `"8o80"`.

{{bare}} First, behind a bare `except`. The code tries to read the port, something goes wrong, and the `except` swallows it and uses the default. The program starts. It listens on the wrong port. Nobody is told anything, and the bug is now a support ticket that says "the site is down" three days later.

{{ctrl}} And while I am here — with a bare `except` inside a loop, `Ctrl-C` does not stop this program. The interrupt is an exception too, and the bare clause caught it.

{{broad}} Second, `except Exception`. Better: `Ctrl-C` works again. But it still catches the `AttributeError` from my own typo on the line below, and reports both of them as "could not read the port". I spend twenty minutes reading configuration files because the message told me to.

{{narrow}} Third, `except ValueError`. Now `int("8o80")` is caught, and nothing else is. The message names the file, the key and the value: `port: "8o80" is not a number`. And the `AttributeError` on the next line is not caught at all — it reaches the traceback, which is where a bug of mine belongs.

{{small}} One more thing to notice. In the third version the `try` holds one line — the `int()` call. In the first it wrapped forty lines, which is why it caught something it was never meant to see.

{{rule}} Catch the narrowest thing you can name, around the smallest block that can raise it, and say something the reader can act on.

Catch what you can answer, and let the rest reach the traceback.

{{question}} The question at every `try` is not "could this fail" — everything could. It is **what would I do here if it did**. A default, another route, a message naming the row. If the honest answer is "nothing useful", then not catching it is the correct decision rather than a missing one.

{{narrow}} Catch the narrowest class you can name. `except Exception` is a wide net for the top of a program, where it exists to log and stop. A bare `except:` catches the interrupt and the exit and is never right.

{{clauses}} `try` holds the thing that fails, and as little else as possible. `else` holds what comes after success, so it is not inside the net. `finally` runs either way, which is what closes the file — and `with` in lesson 9 writes that one for you.

{{raise}} Raise your own with a message a person can act on. `ValueError` when a value is wrong, `TypeError` when the type is, your own class when a caller might want to catch exactly your failure. And `raise … from e` when you are translating one into another, because the original is what says what really happened.
